title: The Thirteen-Minute Call That Closed Convoy
dek: In October 2023 the Seattle trucking start-up shut its core business after a failed sale, and its co-founder told staff there would be no severance.

story.event: Closing the digital freight marketplace's core business and laying off most staff without severance
story.summary: On 19 October 2023 Convoy, the Seattle digital freight marketplace co-founded in 2015 by Dan Lewis and Grant Goodale and valued at $3.8 billion in 2022, closed its core business after more than four months of failing to find a buyer during a freight recession. Most of its roughly 500 remaining staff were laid off without severance, which Lewis said had been taken out of the company's hands by its lenders. Flexport bought Convoy's technology, without its liabilities, on 1 November 2023.
paragraphs: On Thursday 19 October 2023, Dan Lewis spoke to the employees of Convoy, the Seattle trucking marketplace he had co-founded eight years earlier, on a video call that lasted 13 minutes. A memo that day had told most of them it was their last day. "I hoped this day would never come," he said, according to GeekWire, which obtained a recording. "In fact, I really couldn't fathom it." He broke down as he explained that there would be no severance.

Lewis and Grant Goodale, both formerly of Amazon, had founded Convoy in 2015 to match shippers with truckers through software. Investors including Bill Gates and Jeff Bezos put in about $1 billion, and in 2022 a $260 million round, part of it venture debt, valued the company at $3.8 billion. Then freight rates fell from their pandemic highs and investors turned away from unprofitable late-stage companies. Convoy went through four rounds of layoffs in a year, falling from a peak of about 1,500 people to about 500, and closed its Atlanta office.

What Lewis knew that autumn, by his memo, was that the company had spent more than four months looking for a buyer or another way through, and that the most likely acquirers were suffering from the same freight slump. A deal had been lined up and fell through at the last minute, GeekWire's sources said. Convoy was weeks from running out of money. "We were running up the down escalator," Lewis wrote, "and it kept speeding up." Before the doors closed, staff spent several days making sure every shipment already on the road reached its destination.

Severance was the decision he could not make. "In the final hour of this, our ability to make that decision and our available budget was taken away by our lenders," he told staff. Mark Okerstrom, the former Expedia chief executive who had joined Convoy in 2019, asked them to write down an answer for anyone who asked what had happened: "The markets crushed us." Neither man took questions. Less than two weeks later Flexport bought Convoy's technology, but not its liabilities, for an undisclosed sum, and kept a small group of its product and engineering staff.

quote.text: they crush and maim happiness; for they both bring pain with them and hinder many activities. Yet even in these nobility shines through, when a man bears with resignation many great misfortunes, not through insensibility to pain but through nobility and greatness of soul.
quote.source_title: Nicomachean Ethics, tr. W. D. Ross, The Internet Classics Archive (MIT)
quote.connection: Aristotle grants what Okerstrom told staff: great misfortunes do crush. He then places nobility in how misfortune is borne, which leaves an awkward question over Convoy's last day, when much of the weight fell on employees who left without severance.

reflection: The hardest line in this story is not about markets. It is Lewis explaining that the choice to pay people on their way out had passed to his lenders. Some obligations can be honoured only while you still control the money, and they are easiest to protect long before the last hour.

You are a long way from that kind of room. Even so, it is worth knowing, in calm times, what you would want to guarantee the people who work with you if things went wrong, and which agreements might quietly take that out of your hands.
invitation: Pick one agreement you have signed or are about to sign, and read only the part that says who decides what happens if things go badly.

research_notes: Total funding: GeekWire says around $1 billion; Bloomberg (via Fortune), citing PitchBook, says more than $1 billion; the story says about $1 billion. The 2022 round: CNBC says $260 million led by Baillie Gifford and Hercules Capital; GeekWire says it included $100 million of venture debt from Hercules; the story says part of it was venture debt. Layoff rounds: GeekWire counts four in the past year, CNBC says multiple. The severance account rests on GeekWire's report of the recorded call, including Lewis's own statement blaming the lenders' control of the budget; it is attributed to him and not stated as fact. GeekWire reports that the farewell statement 'I hoped this day would never come' was said on the call; the memo itself used 'We hoped'. The failed last-minute deal comes from GeekWire's unnamed sources and is attributed. The memo's 'running up the down escalator…. and it kept speeding up' is quoted in two parts around 'Lewis wrote'; nothing is omitted between them. Okerstrom's title is given as in GeekWire (former Expedia CEO who joined in 2019); his exact Convoy title is not relied on. The Flexport price was undisclosed; a later unverified estimate is not used. GeekWire blocks automated requests, so Internet Archive copies are cited. Lewis's later work is outside this episode and not covered. The Aristotle passage is about the effect of great misfortunes on a happy life; it is applied by analogy.
